paper_title: TARGET Benchmarking Table Retrieval for Generative Tasks
caption: Influence of k on retrieval performance with various baselines on the FeTaQA dataset, confirming the expectation that performance gradually increases with k, most significantly for dense embedding approaches.

model_annotations.Bulgarian:
The provided line chart illustrates how retrieval performance, measured by recall, varies with the parameter k across five different baseline methods on the FeTaQA dataset. The x-axis represents the value of k, ranging from 0 to approximately 50, with labeled tick marks at intervals of 20 (i.e., 0, 20, 40). The y-axis represents recall, scaled linearly from 0.0 to 0.8, with labeled tick marks at intervals of 0.2 (i.e., 0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8). The unit for recall is dimensionless, as is standard for this metric.

The chart displays five distinct lines, each corresponding to a different baseline method as indicated by the legend:
- A light gray line with circular markers represents “sparse lexical repr. (w/ title)”. It starts at a recall of approximately 0.0 and increases gradually to about 0.2.
- A purple dashed line with circular markers represents “sparse lexical repr. (w/o title)”. It starts at a recall of approximately 0.0 and increases slightly to about 0.2.
- A red dashed line with circular markers represents “dense table emb. (col names only)”. It starts at a recall of approximately 0.1 and increases to about 0.4.
- A teal line with circular markers represents “dense metadata emb.”. It starts at a recall of approximately 0.25 and increases to about 0.6.
- A dark blue line with circular markers represents “dense row emb.”. It starts at a recall of approximately 0.45 and increases to about 0.85.

All lines show a general upward trend as k increases, with the dense embedding methods (“dense table emb.”, “dense metadata emb.”, and “dense row emb.”) achieving significantly higher recall values than the sparse lexical representations. The “dense row emb.” method consistently achieves the highest recall across all values of k, followed by “dense metadata emb.” and then “dense table emb.”. The “sparse lexical repr.” methods show the lowest recall values and exhibit the smallest increase in performance as k increases.
